sentences.text: The rule about the seal was not written down anywhere and everybody in the bay knew it exactly.
You saw her once.
Not once a year, not once a season — once, in a life, and then never again, and the once was not at a time of your choosing.
And you did not go looking, because looking did not work, and everybody had an uncle who had spent a summer proving it.
Maeve knew the rule the way she knew that the harbour steps were slippy on the fourth one from the bottom.
She had never been told it in a single sitting.
It had assembled itself out of twelve years of overheard sentences at the co-op and on the pier and in the back of the van.
What she had noticed, and what nobody talked about, was the shape of when it happened.
Mr Nolan had seen her the winter he lost the *Bright Star*, three days before the insurance came through.
The Coyle brothers had both seen her, separately, in the same week, which was the week their mother was in Sligo hospital.
The woman who ran the chandlery had seen her on the morning she had decided to sell the chandlery, and had not sold it.
Maeve made a list once, in a maths copybook, of the thirteen sightings she could get people to be specific about.
Then she wrote what had been going on for that person at the time, which took longer and involved asking questions that made two adults change the subject.
She looked at the list for a while.
Then she wrote, at the bottom, in small letters: *she comes when you are about to stop.* She did not show it to anyone.
It is still in the copybook and the copybook is still in the drawer under the stairs.
There were two things about the list that she did not write down.
The first was that in every single case, the person had carried on.
Mr Nolan had bought the second boat, which everyone agreed was a worse boat.
The Coyles had kept fishing through the whole of their mother's illness and after it.
The chandlery was still there, with the same woman in it, still complaining about the same suppliers.
That could have meant that the seal changed something.

It could also have meant that she only came to people who were going to carry on anyway, and that the ones who really stopped never saw her, and that nobody had ever thought to count those because a person who leaves a place stops appearing in the conversations of that place.
There was no list of the people who had gone.
There could not be.
That was the whole difficulty with it.
Maeve turned this over for most of a winter and could not find a way to test it, and it bothered her in a way she has never entirely got rid of.
The second thing was smaller and worse.
Her father had seen the seal.
Everybody knew he had.
It was said about him the way you say a man is left-handed — a settled fact, mentioned in passing, of no particular weight.
And in twelve years nobody had ever once said when.
